newsitem.title: FRANCE: France's Chirac to Belgium for industry, EU talks.
newsitem.headline: France's Chirac to Belgium for industry, EU talks.

text.p: French President Jacques Chirac visits Belgium on Wednesday for talks likely to be dominated by industrial frictions and by Europe's plans for a single currency from 1999.

Brussels, often ill at ease with its big southern neighbour, has strongly criticised Paris over the planned closure of a Renault car plant in Belgium and France's refusal so far to hand over secret documents to Belgian investigators in a bribery case.

Chirac will hold talks with Belgian Prime Minister Jean-Luc Dehaene after his arrival on Wednesday afternoon, also discussing issues like NATO enlargement and European Union border controls, officials say.
King Albert is to give a dinner in Chirac's honour on Wednesday. On Thursday, Chirac is to meet European Commission President Jacques Santer.
In a Bastille Day address on Monday, Chirac warned of "very serious consequences" if the EU scrapped plans for a single currency -- a project to which both Chirac and Dehaene are strongly committed.

Talks with Dehaene may be strained after Brussels' criticisms of French carmaker Renault's plans to close the Vilvoorde car plant in Belgium, which employs 3,100 people. The French state is the biggest shareholder in Renault with 46 percent.

Dehaene said new Socialist Prime Minister Lionel Jospin misled the Renault staff during campaigning for France's parliamentary election on June 1. Belgium wants job creation measures to compensate for layoffs.
During the campaign, Jospin promised to review the closure but has not stopped it.

Jospin's government also said last month it was reviewing whether to hand Belgium secret documents to help a bribery probe against French warplane maker Serge Dassault. The former centre-right government refused to hand over the documents.
An official at the French Justice Ministry said that a decision seemed unlikely during Chirac's visit. "It's still under review," the official said.

Belgian police are investigating accusations that Dassault Aviation paid 600 million Belgian francs ($17 million) to political parties to secure a contract to fit air defence systems to Belgian F-16 jets in the last 1980s.

In another potential flashpoint, France's state-owned arms group GIAT Industries is aiming to sell its 92 percent stake in Belgium's Herstal SA to U.S. gunmaker Colt. Belgian unions fear it could spell more job losses for their workers.

Paris and Brussels are also at odds over France's decision to maintain land border controls against Belgium and Luxembourg despite the EU's so-called Schengen pact aimed at creating a border-free zone.

France says drug smugglers pass through the two countries from the Netherlands, which Paris accuses of having lax policies. Yet France has lifted border controls with Germany, its main EU ally, meaning traffickers can take a longer route from the Netherlands to France via Germany and avoid checks.
